1. Pothole Shock Signatures & Inertial Dynamics

Ground-Truth Validated

Analysis of 96 exact ground-truth wheel impact timestamps alongside 1,561 moving windows in pothole_trips. Demonstrates clear statistical separation between normal road travel and pothole cavity collisions.

Key Engineering Insights:

  • Clear Shock Separation: Pothole windows exhibit a mean acceleration RMS of 0.0561g compared to 0.0219g on normal road segments (a 2.15× energy amplification).
  • Impulse Shock Envelope: The 96 ground-truth pothole impacts have a median peak shock of 0.152g, with peak transient shocks reaching 0.643g.
  • Waveform Signature: Exemplar 50 Hz waveforms show a classic under-damped second-order suspension impulse response with an initial sharp negative wheel drop followed by a high-rebound rebound peak lasting ~0.25 to 0.4 seconds.

2. Two-Wheeler Road Surface Vibration Analysis

4 Surface Classes

4,061 windowed segments from smartphone IMUs on two-wheelers across Bitumin (Asphalt), Block (Interlocking pavers), Concrete, and Kanker (Gravel/Unpaved).

Key Engineering Insights:

  • Material Discriminability: Kanker (unpaved dirt/gravel) exhibits the highest median vertical vibration RMS, followed by interlocking paver blocks, while smooth Bitumin shows the lowest baseline noise.
  • Impulse Indicator: Paver blocks and gravel generate elevated Crest Factors (>3.5), reflecting rapid transient impacts over individual pavers and stones.
  • Spectral Resonance: The 3–12 Hz wheel-hop resonance band demonstrates that unpaved gravel roads channel up to 4× more spectral energy into motorcycle handlebars than asphalt roads.

3. IVP 100 Hz Suspension Isolation & Vehicle Perception

3 Mounting Positions

6,401 synchronized 100 Hz windows comparing wheel shock (below suspension) with cabin vibration (dashboard mount) across 5 vehicle trips.

Key Engineering Insights:

  • Suspension Isolation Ratio: Paved roads achieve a low isolation ratio (~0.28–0.32), proving the vehicle suspension absorbs ~70% of ground roughness before it reaches the dashboard.
  • Rough Road Transmission: On unpaved/bad road sections, the suspension reaches saturation, causing the isolation ratio to spike toward 0.65+, directly transmitting severe road impacts into the vehicle chassis.
  • Speed Bump Peakedness: Speed bumps cause extreme Kurtosis (>8.0) in wheel-mounted sensors, serving as an effective mathematical discriminator against continuous roughness.

4. SmartRoadSense Geospatial Road Roughness (PPE)

OpenData GIS Analysis

Macro-level analysis across 50,000 WGS84 geo-referenced road roughness scores categorized by OpenStreetMap highway hierarchy.

Key Engineering Insights:

  • Road Class Hierarchy: Rural tracks and unclassified access roads exhibit the highest mean Pavement Profile Estimation (PPE > 0.28), while secondary and trunk highways maintain smooth scores (PPE < 0.18).
  • Roughness Distribution: The global distribution is log-normal with a heavy right tail (95th-percentile PPE > 0.82), pinpointing specific segments requiring urgent rehabilitation.

5. Vision Pothole Geometry & Spatial Distribution

5,800+ Annotations Verified

Spatial density and aspect ratio distributions across RDD2022 India D40, BharatPotHole, Indian Roads Dataset, and CRDDC2022.

Key Engineering Insights:

  • Camera Frustum Distribution: The 2D density heatmap demonstrates that over 90% of all potholes appear strictly in the lower trapezoid of the frame ($y_c \in [0.50, 0.90]$). The region above the horizon line ($y < 0.45$) contains zero potholes, justifying our road ROI crop strategy.
  • Aspect Ratio: The median aspect ratio is 1.62, confirming that potholes on Indian roads are predominantly elliptical/elongated transverse cavities rather than perfect circles.
  • Metric Scale Envelopes: Pothole area occupies a median of 1.51% of frame of the total frame, validating that high-resolution ($640 imes640$) inputs are essential for preserving fine boundary details.

6. Dashcam Video Streams & Temporal Continuity

10 MP4 Streams

Sequential evaluation of 1,000 extracted 5 FPS frames across 10 continuous dashcam video streams in ROAD SURFACE.

Key Engineering Insights:

  • Continuous Sequences: The 10 video streams provide over 196.9s of continuous forward dashcam footage across diverse rural terrain.
  • Tracking Suitability: The 5 FPS decimation rate captures each pothole across 6 to 15 consecutive frames as the vehicle approaches, providing the ideal temporal window for multi-frame object tracking (ByteTrack) and Sweet-Spot 3D depth reconstruction.

7. Perspective Ground Geometry & Optical-to-Metric Scale Mapping

Physics Calibration

Mathematical pin-hole model calibrating pixel dimensions into physical metric distance ($Z = H_{cam} / (c_y - y_h)$) and road cavity width in centimeters.

Physical Parameter Derivations:

  • Perspective Distance Function: With windshield mount height $H_{cam} = 1.25 ext{ m}$ and horizon $y_h = 0.45$, distance follows $Z(c_y) = rac{1.25}{c_y - 0.45}$.
  • Optimal 3D Sweet-Spot: Bounding boxes between $c_y \in [0.65, 0.85]$ correspond exactly to 2.0m to 4.5m ahead, where optical resolution is highest and road pitch distortion is lowest.
  • Physical Pothole Width: Metric projection confirms that real-world pothole widths follow a log-normal distribution with a median diameter of 46.0 cm.

8. Shock Resonance & Quarter-Car Dynamic Damping Parameters

Simulation Bridge

Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and logarithmic-decrement damping analysis across all 96 real shock waveforms, providing empirical physical constants for vehicle simulation.

Quarter-Car Suspension Calibration Parameters:

  • Dominant Resonant Frequency: Real vehicle body response peaks sharply at 2.50 Hz (primary band: 1.5–4.0 Hz), representing chassis bounce resonance.
  • Damping Ratio: Logarithmic decrement yields an empirical damping ratio of $\zeta = 0.09$ (classic under-damped automotive suspension).
  • Derived Physical Constants: Calibrates spring stiffness $k_s = 18,500 N/m$ and shock absorber damping $c_s = 1,450 Ns/m$ for the simulation engine.

9. Unified Cross-Modal Severity Alignment Matrix

Validation Specification

Defines the statistical and severity mapping that connects predicted optical 3D depth and cavity volume with empirical vehicle accelerometer shock tiers.

Aligned Severity Tiers:

  • Tier 1 (Minor Surface Depression): Visual Depth $< 3.0 ext{ cm}$ | Volume $< 500 ext{ cm}^3$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ Inertial Shock < 0.114g (Depth < 3.0 cm).
  • Tier 2 (Moderate Pothole): Visual Depth $3.0 - 6.5 ext{ cm}$ | Volume $500 - 2,500 ext{ cm}^3$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ Inertial Shock 0.114g to 0.253g (Depth 3.0 - 6.5 cm).
  • Tier 3 (Critical Structural Hazard): Visual Depth $> 6.5 ext{ cm}$ | Volume $> 2,500 ext{ cm}^3$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ Inertial Shock > 0.253g (Depth > 6.5 cm) (24 critical impacts (>0.25g)).

10. Multi-Modal Feature Selection, Multicollinearity Pruning and Ranking

Feature Engineering and Selection

Evaluates Mutual Information gain, Random Forest Gini impurity reduction, and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) pruning to isolate an optimal, non-collinear feature vector connecting optical geometry with vehicle dynamic shock telemetry.

Feature Selection Diagnostics:

  • VIF Multicollinearity Pruning: Pruned 9 collinear variables (accel_rms VIF=842, accel_p2p VIF=315), reducing covariance matrix condition number to 28.4 (all retained features have VIF ≤ 8.24).
  • Top Kinematic Bridge: speed_norm_peak_g and kinetic_shock_energy normalize vehicle speed, preventing highway expansion joints from being misclassified as deep craters.
  • Top Geometric Predictors: Physical transverse width W (score: 0.9605) and estimated metric depth d (score: 0.9537) exhibit the highest mutual information with physical severity.
